Hi Andrei,

In a nutshell, a decreasing index sequence won't work in model code.  In this case, it would be desirable for your example to work.  In general, model code needs to be processed more intricately to correctly determine the graph of model relationships, which creates more stringent checking and trapping.   Your workaround with nimConvolution is a good solution.

A secondary issue is that in model code, the sequence must take the form (start index):(end index).  For example, it can't take the form "offset + (start index):(end index)".   We just added a message to that effect to the devel branch yesterday.

-Perry

Hi Mahdieh,

This is a case where you can use a user-defined distribution. Please
see Section 12.2 of the manual. Given that there is an example of
writing a simple exponential distribution there, hopefully it will be
straightforward for you to write the ddexp case.

You could also, without having to define your own distribution, write
the double exponential as a scale mixture of normals using a parameter
augmentation approach, but this introduces additional parameters so
would likely decrease MCMC efficiency. So I'd suggest the user-defined
distribution approach.

Filling out some of the extra distributions that we have said we'd
like to add always seems to take lower priority than other things
we're doing, but given your interest and that this case is a common
one, hopefully we can add this as part of NIMBLE in the next release
or two.
Chris

messages.subject: Smoother 1D CAR Process in NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Smoother 1D CAR Process in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am currently working on a discrete-time series model where I would like a relatively smooth temporal process in the mean. The model is for epidemiological forecasting and involves the last few data being missing so that they can be predicted. I started using a penalised cubic spline set up with GAM, which was very efficient (good sampling after 1000 iterations of burn-in) but I feel it is inappropriate because, in the missing region at the end of the time series, the combination of the lack of data and the smoothing penalty meant that the spline just continued whatever trend it had before the missing data.

I have also tried using a multivariate normal process with a squared exponential or a matern covariance function of temporal distance, which produced an ideal process but was very inefficient using the default RW_block sampler, requiring 1 million samples of burn-in. I tried using an AF_slice sampler which worked better but it was not reliable, often reaching the maximum number of contractions. I don't really know why this happens despite adding a small amount to the diagonal of the covariance matrix to make it more numerically stable. Has anyone had this issue for gaussian processes using these samplers?

Sigma[1:N,1:N] <- exp(-(dist[1:N,1:N]/rho)^2)*sigma^2 + 0.0001*diag(N)
delta[1:N] ~ dmnorm(zero[1:N],cov=Sigma[1:N,1:N])
sigma ~ T(dnorm(0,1),0,)
rho ~ dlnorm(2,1)

My most recent attempt is to base the process on an improper CAR prior in one dimension, hoping to emulate a thin plate spline like the 'rw2' model in INLA. I tried setting order=2 in dcar_normal, as suggested in the manual, without changing any of the weights. However, this still results in quite a coarse process:

adj=c(2,as.numeric(rbind(1:(N-2),3:N)),N-1)
n_adj=c(1,rep(2,N-2),1)

delta[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj=adj[1:l_adj],num=n_adj[1:N],tau=nu,c=2,zero_mean=1)
sigma ~ T(dnorm(0,1),0,)
nu <- 1/sigma^2

To achieve a smoother CAR process, should I provide the model with a different adjacency structure and weights? Alternatively, does anyone have any suggestions for how to more efficiently implement a more appropriate temporal process in NIMBLE?

Thanks,

Oliver

messages.subject_clean: Smoother 1D CAR Process in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Oliver, a couple options for the second-order smoothing:

1) if you look at the 'ice' model in the original BUGS examples (available in the classic-bugs/vol2/ice directory in the installed NIMBLE package) you'll see how to specify a 2nd-order random walk directly by conditioning on the past rather than using the CAR representation.  There's also some discussion of this example in the http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Ice.html.

The representation above is equivalent to an IID model on the second differences in time. (Whereas a first-order model is equivalent to an IID model on first differences.)

2) As far as the CAR representation for a second order model, Section 6.3 of the classic Breslow and Clayton 1993 paper (https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/2290687.pdf)  discusses the CAR formulation relative to the conditioning on the past formulation. There is also info in this tutorial I wrote: https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~paciorek/research/techVignettes/techVignette5.pdf.

So to implement that in NIMBLE: you need to have each time point have as neighbors the nearest two time points in both the future and the past (with fewer neighbors for points at or within one time point of the boundary). And the weights should be what is given in the Breslow and Clayton reference (or in the Rue & Held Gaussian Markov Random Fields book, Section 3.4, equation 3.40). So you'd have  this inputs for the dcar_normal specification, for an example of 6 time points:

adj = c(2, 3, 1, 3, 4, 1, 2, 4, 5, 2, 3, 5, 6, 3, 4, 6, 4, 5)
## weights are negative of the non-zero values show in the Breslow/Clayton and Rue/Held refs, with the diagonals ignored:
weights = c(2, -1, 2, 4, -1, -1, 4, 4, -1, -1, 4, 4, -1, -1, 4, 2, -1 , 2)
num = c(2, 3, 4, 4, 3, 2)
c = 2
zero_mean = 0

That said, I suspect the simple representation in #1 above will mix just as well or better and is simpler to implement and explain.

I'm somewhat surprised the RW_block does as poorly as you found. However squared exponential and Matern with large "nu" parameter (say bigger than 3-4) gives very smooth processes that can strongly constrain neighboring values when sampling (which could still be the case if the amount added to the diagonal is rather small). So that can slow mixing. It might also be that you need to carefully specify the initial proposal covariance matrix - e.g., making sure that the proposal variances are all reasonable.

-Chris

Oliver, apologies for the over-sight not allowing negative weights in the dcar_normal distribution. Until our next updated release of NIMBLE, you can install the development branch from GitHub (which includes these changes) using:

> remove.packages('nimble')
> library(devtools)
> install_github('nimble-dev/nimble', ref = 'devel', subdir = 'packages/nimble')
> library(nimble)

Please let me know if you have a chance to try this out, and whether or not it solves your problem.

Cheers,
Daniel

Thanks for fixing it so quickly. It does seem to have fixed the problem. Thanks again for the advice and the quick fix. I'm now going to try to replace my cyclic cubic spline which captures the seasonal patterns with a cyclic second-order CAR.

Oliver

messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrei,

When you switch from using scalar x[1], x[2], ... variables to the
vector x[1:K], the sampler(s) assigned by NIMBLE change from slice
samplers on each x[i] to a random walk block sampler. Our slice
sampler recognizes that x[i] are discrete and proposes new values
appropriately.  Our random walk block sampler is not designed for
discrete multivariate random variables and so proposes non-integer
values and you get the warnings you do.  A simple fix is to configure
the MCMC so that each x[i] is sampled using a slice sampler. But that
presumably defeats the purpose of creating the vectorized binomial
density since each scalar sampler will recompute the likelihood for
the full vector x[1:K].

We don't have a sampler in our provided samplers that would handle
this discrete multivariate case, so if you wanted to continue on this
path, you would probably need to write your own multivariate sampler
for x[1:K]. This could be a version of our RW_block sampler (you can
copy and then modify the sampler_RW_block code from the file
MCMC_samplers.R in https://github.com/nimble-devnimble) that proposes
integer-valued proposals perhaps via some sort of rounding. There is
discussion of user-defined samplers in Section 5 of chapter 15 of the
NIMBLE manual.

All that being said, there is a bigger issue here. In the form you
write your model, NIMBLE is not constraining y[1:K,1:K] such that the
rowSums are equal to the values of observed. To impose such a
constraint, you need to use the dconstraint() syntax discussed in
Section 5.2.7.3 of the NIMBLE manual. And once you do impose the
constraint, MCMC sampling won't work very well (actually it probably
won't accept any proposals at all) because it will be very hard for a
sampler to propose values of 'y' that are consistent with the fixed
values of 'observed'. I think you would have to come up with your own
user-defined sampler that proposed new 'y' values that are consistent
with 'observed'. E.g., within a row of 'y', you could propose to
increase one element by one and decrease another element by one so the
sum stays fixed.

Chris

    secondexpo_b <- numeric(length = s)
    secondexpo <- numeric(length = s)
    thirdexpo <- numeric(length = s-1)
    fourthexpo <- numeric(length = s)
    fifthexpo <- numeric(length = s)
    sixthexpo <- numeric(length = s)
    ##### constants for the first occasion
    secondexpo_a[1] <- u[1]

    secondexpo_b[1] <- 0
    secondexpo[1] <- secondexpo_a[1] - secondexpo_b[1] - n[1]
    thirdexpo[1] <- sum(v[2:s])
    fourthexpo[1] <- n[1]-d[1]
    fifthexpo[1] <- sum(u[2:s])
    sixthexpo[1] <- v[1]-d[1]

    secondexpo_b[s] <- sum(v[1:(s-1)])
    secondexpo[s] <- secondexpo_a[s] - secondexpo_b[s] - n[s]
    fourthexpo[s] <- n[s]-d[s]
    fifthexpo[s] <- 0
    sixthexpo[s] <- v[s]-d[s]

      # first exponent
    firstexpo[i] <- sum(u[1:(i-1)])
    # second exponent
    secondexpo_a[i] <- sum(u[1:i])
    secondexpo_b[i] <- sum(v[1:(i-1)])
    secondexpo[i] <- secondexpo_a[i] - secondexpo_b[i] - n[i]
    # third exponent
    thirdexpo[i] <- sum(v[(i+1):s])
    # fourth exponent
    fourthexpo[i] <- n[i]-d[i]
    # fifth exponent

    for (i in 2:s) {

      gamma[i] <- (phi[i-1] / rho[i-1])
      gamma_constr[i] <- min(gamma[i],1)
    }

      (fourthexpo[s] * log(mu[s])) + (d[s] * log(1-mu[s])) + (fifthexpo[s] * log(1-(p[s]*(1-mu[s])))) +
      (sixthexpo[s] * log(chi[s]))

    ##### log-likelihood from occasion 2 to s-1

    for (i in 2:(s-1)) {
      l.num[i] <- (u[i] * log(xi[i])) + (firstexpo[i] * (log(phi[i-1]) - log(rho[i-1]))) + (n[i] * log(p[i])) + (secondexpo[i] * log(1-p[i])) +
        (thirdexpo[i] * log(phi[i])) + (fourthexpo[i] * log(mu[i])) + (d[i] * log(1-mu[i])) + (fifthexpo[i] * log(1-(p[i]*(1-mu[i])))) +

    }

      ##### likelihood denominator

      PROD1[1] <- 1

        PROD1_tmp[1,j] <- 0
      }
      # fill part of PROD1_tmp
      for (i in 2:(s-1)) {
        for (j in i:(s-1)){
          PROD1_tmp[i,j] <- 0
        }
      }
      for (i in 2:s) {
        for (j in 1:(i-1)){
          PROD1_tmp[i,j] <- phi[j] * (1-(p[j]*(1-mu[j])))
        }
      }

      for (i in 3:s) {
        PROD1[i] <- prod(PROD1_tmp[i,1:(i-1)])
      }
      # 2nd product
      PROD2[s] <- 1
      for (i in 1:(s-1)) {
        for (j in (i+1):s) {
          PROD2_tmp[i,j] <- gamma[j]
        }
      }
      # fill part of PROD2_tmp
      for (i in 1:(s-1)) {

        for (j in 1:i) {
          PROD2_tmp[i,j] <- 0
        }
      }
      PROD2[s-1] <- PROD2_tmp[(s-1),s]

      }
      for (i in 1:s) {

      }

    }

Unfortunately, nimbleFunctions with setup code can't be used in models.

One work-around is to embed the vectors you create in the setup code into the model itself.  Even if they aren't part of the model from a statistical point of view, putting them into the model makes it possible to pass them to a nimbleFunction used in the model. For example, you should be able to say

x ~ condL(phi[1:T], <other model variables>..., expos[1:8, 1:s])

Then set up the expos in R (To keep it short, I assumed you could pack the eight "expo" variables into a matrix, but you could keep them separate) and provide them to the model as data (or constants; it shouldn't matter).  They'll be passed to condL every time it is called.

Another option would be to use a nimbleExternalCall to call a C function you would write for condL.  In the C code you could arrange access to the constants ("expo" variables) you need.

The run function will be a bit faster if you use numeric(length = s, init = FALSE) when you do not need to rely on initialization with zeros.  It was surprising, but I once clocked a noticeable performance improvement by avoiding unnecessary initialization.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to see if I can implement Kalman filtering of global temperature (two different datasets, attached) in Shumway and Stoffer (https://www.stat.pitt.edu/stoffer/tsa4/tsa4.pdf, Page 304) using NIMBLE.

In particular, I am trying to run the Liu and West filter, since it can sample from the posterior distribution of top-level parameters as well as latent states.

The model is simple as shown in  Shumway and Stoffer:

xt = d + xt−1 + wt, where xt is the state variable and d is a drift.

yt = Axt + vt,  where yt = [yt1, yt2]^T, A = [1,1]^T and vt = [vt1, vt2]^T

However, the values I get from the LW filter is quite different (most likely wrong) from those of Shumway and Stoffer. Estimates with standard error from Shumway and Stoffer are (as in the book):

estimate SE

sigw: 0.055, 0.011

cR11 (Cholesky decomposition): 0.074, 0.010

cR22: 0.127, 0.015

cR12: 0.129, 0.038

drift: 0.006, 0.005

Please see my initial code (priors are somewhat arbitrary at this moment) and offer any thoughts or correct my mistakes.

Thanks very much in advance!

- Seongeun

-------------

load ('globtemp.rda')

load ('globtempl.rda')

y = cbind (globtemp, globtempl)

## define the model

#xt = δ + xt−1 + wt

stateSpaceCode <- nimbleCode({

# drift

d ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)

sigw ~ T(dnorm (0, 10), 0.0001, )

x[1] ~ dnorm(-0.35, sd = 1)

y[1,1] ~ dnorm(mean = x[1], sd = 10)

y[1,2] ~ dnorm(mean = x[1], sd = 10)

for (i in 2:t) {

#xt = d + xt−1 + wt

x[i] ~ dnorm(x[i - 1] + d, sd = sigw)

X [1] <- x[i - 1]

X [2] <- x[i - 1]

# observation model: yt = Axt + vt,

# where yt = [yt1, yt2]^T, A = [1,1]^T and vt = [vt1, vt2]^T

y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

}

# observation noise

R[1,1] <- pow (r11,2)

R[1,2] <- pow (r12,2)

R[2,1] <- pow (r12,2)

R[2,2] <- pow (r22,2)

r11 ~ T(dt(mu = 0, sigma = 1, df=1), 0, 100)

r12 ~ T(dt(mu = 0, sigma = 1, df=1), 0, 100)

r22 ~ T(dt(mu = 0, sigma = 1, df=1), 0, 100)

})

## define data, constants, and initial values

data <- list(

y = y

)

constants <- list(

t = nrow (y)

)

inits <- list(

r11 = .1,

r12 = .1,

r22 = .1,

d = 0,

sigw = 0.05)

## build the model

stateSpaceModel <- nimbleModel(stateSpaceCode,

data = data,

constants = constants,

inits = inits,

check = FALSE)

LWTimeModel <- stateSpaceModel

compileNimble(LWTimeModel)

rLWF <- buildLiuWestFilter(LWTimeModel, "x", params = c('r11', 'r12', 'r22', 'sigw', 'd'),

control = list(saveAll = FALSE))

cLWF <- compileNimble(rLWF,project = LWTimeModel)

cLWF$run(1000)

> When you switch from using scalar x[1], x[2], ... variables to the

> samplers on each x[i] to a random walk block sampler. Our slice
> sampler recognizes that x[i] are discrete and proposes new values
> appropriately.  Our random walk block sampler is not designed for
> discrete multivariate random variables and so proposes non-integer
> values and you get the warnings you do.  A simple fix is to configure
> the MCMC so that each x[i] is sampled using a slice sampler. But that
> presumably defeats the purpose of creating the vectorized binomial
> density since each scalar sampler will recompute the likelihood for
> the full vector x[1:K].
>
> We don't have a sampler in our provided samplers that would handle
> this discrete multivariate case, so if you wanted to continue on this
> path, you would probably need to write your own multivariate sampler
> for x[1:K]. This could be a version of our RW_block sampler (you can
> copy and then modify the sampler_RW_block code from the file
> MCMC_samplers.R in https://github.com/nimble-devnimble) that proposes
> integer-valued proposals perhaps via some sort of rounding. There is
> discussion of user-defined samplers in Section 5 of chapter 15 of the
> NIMBLE manual.

messages.body_plain:
I am attempting to fit a Hidden Markov Model to the GPS locations of a small forest carnivore. I have a version of the model I want to fit running in Stan, but I wanted to give NIMBLE a try because I don't think that Stan will be able to fit the full model I want to fit. Specifically, I am interested in modeling the movement of an animal that switches between resting and active movement. In this model, when the animal is resting the difference between subsequent GPS locations is purely due to observation error, when the animal is not resting the difference between two locations is modeled in terms of the step length and turning angle between two points measured with observation error.

The attached code summarizes my progress in building up to the model I am attempting to fit. So far I have been successful in:

Including and fitting the von Mises distribution for turning angles
Fitting a simple "single-state" correlated random walk
Including observation error in the correlated random walk
However, I have encountered difficulties in including the state switching in my simulated examples for two cases. My goal eventually is to merge these two cases into the final model.

Case 1:
In the first case, I have attempted to model a standard Hidden Markov Model  for animal movement without observation error. That is, the observed step-length and turning angle depend on the state the animal is in during each timestep and the probability of switching of remaining in the same state in the next timestep is determined by a transition matrix. Rather than marginalizing ("filtering"), I have attempted to model the state as an unobserved discrete variable. I know with this formulation that I can marginalize over the latent states, but hopefully my second case will show why I do not want to do that. When I attempt to fit the code from the first case to simulated data, I get a series of errors from NIMBLE all related to the latent discrete variable z.

Error in envRefInferField(x, what, getClass(class(x)), selfEnv) :
  ‘i’ is not a valid field or method name for reference class “code_MID_77_modelClass_UID_971_UID_972”
Note: cannot calculate logProb for node  z[999] .

The model and simulation code for the first case is in the attached, but for the casual reader here is the code of the model:

switching_CRW <- nimbleCode({
  pi <- 3.141593
  shape[1] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  shape[2] ~ dgamma(2, 1)
  rate[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  rate[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  loc[1] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  loc[2] ~ dunif(-pi, pi)
  kappa[1] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )
  kappa[2] ~ T(dnorm(5, sd = 1), 0, )
  remain[1] ~ dbeta(9, 1)
  remain[2] ~ dbeta(1, 9)
  alpha[1, 1] <- remain_1
  alpha[1, 2] <- 1 - remain_1
  alpha[2, 1] <- 1 - remain_2
  alpha[2, 2] <- remain_2
  lambda[1] ~ dunif(0, 1)
  lambda[2] <- 1 - lambda[1]
  phi[1, 1] <- lambda[1]
  phi[1, 2] <- lambda[2]

  z[1] ~ dcat(phi[1, 1:2])

  steps[1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[1]], rate[z[1]])
  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc[z[1]], kappa[z[1]])

  for (i in 3:N) {
    z[i - 1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i - 2], 1:2])
    steps[i - 1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[i - 1]], rate[z[i - 1]])
    turn_angle[i - 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[i - 2] + loc[z[i - 1]], kappa[z[i - 1]])
  }
})

Case 2:
In the second case, I am attempting to model the switching between a "resting" state and a moving state with observation error. In this case, the discrete state variable is known and included in the model as data. I don't get any errors from this model, rather it seems to fail at the configuration step. When I use nimbleMCMC, I get the following messages, but the MCMC does not run and the mcmc.out object is not saved to the environment:

defining model...
building model...
setting data and initial values...
running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ...

Hi Dalton,

Thanks for the questions.

Your first problem seems to reveal a bug in how valid range limits are checked for the dcat.  As a workaround,  please try removing the dcat line for z[i-1] and using the following equivalent code:

While this is an unfortunate boundary to run into, it does reflect that the model as written could be really inefficient.  This happens in state-space models where random effects are propagated through a long series of deterministic state calculations.  For example, in your model, for a sampler to update a value of turn_angle[3] (to pick one), it will need to calculate *all* of x[4]...x[N], y[4]...y[N], and log probabilities of xo[4]...xo[N] and yo[4]...yo[N]. x[2:N] <- calculate_xs(x[1:N], turn_angle[1:N], steps[1:N], z[1:N])
and write calculate_xs as a nimbleFunction to calculate the entire series of locations.  In nimble, this will replace 999 scalar nodes with 1 vector node.  If you take that route, you  might as well represent x and y locations jointly in a 2xN matrix and calculate them jointly.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry

  rate[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, sd = 1), 0, )

  turn_angle[1] ~ dvonm(loc[z[1]], kappa[z[1]])

    z[i + 1] ~ dcat(alpha[z[i], 1:2])
    steps[i + 1] ~ dgamma(shape[z[i]], rate[z[i]])
    turn_angle[i + 1] ~ dvonm(turn_angle[i] + loc[z[i]], kappa[z[i]])
  }
})

I'm not sure I following your second suggestion. The problem with writing the x[i] and y[i] as stochastic is that the random variable for the hidden states is on the difference between two locations. This parameterization in terms of step lengths and turning angles is fairly common in the animal movement world and makes it more convenient to look at covariates (for example attraction/repulsion from certain landscape features). But that means that in order to connect the movement process to the locations, one needs to

I'm looking into an alternative model specification based on a bivariate normal (see Jonsen et al. 2004 <https://www.jstor.org/stable/3450801?seq=1#metadata_info_tab_contents>) that would allow me to more easily write the x[i], y[i] as stochastic when the animal is moving, (i.e. loc[t + 1,1:2] ~ dmnorm(loc[t, 1:2] + ..., sd = Sigma), where loc[t,1]  = x[t]), but this tricky business of including the resting state means that I still need to figure out a way for this to be deterministic when the animal is the resting state. That is, loc[t+1, 1:2] = loc[t, 1:2] when z[t] == 1.

This is a tricky problem it seems. There are good algorithms for calculating the log-likelihood for hidden markov models without observation error, and good algorithms for observation error in a state space model, but only for a single behavior state. But it seems really tricky to combine the two. Especially with this "resting" state which is basically a zero inflation on the hidden state update.

If I may change the subject briefly back to the Hidden Markov example though. How would I go about encoding the initial state as distributed according to the stationary distribution? That is in my code above and in my simulated example for it, I have that remain[1] = 0.95 and remain[2] = 0.9. Thus alpha is a 2x2 matrix [[0.95, 0.05], [0.1, 0.9]]. The model successfully estimates these parameter correctly now. It also correctly estimates lambda[1] = 0.33..., and lambda[2] = 0.66... but this is a consequence of the Z[1] being distributed according to the stationary distribution which is:

matrix(c(1,1), nrow = 1) %*% inverse((diag(c(1,1)) - alpha+ matrix(c(1,1,1,1), nrow = 2)))

I spent some more time to figure out what's happening here.

The bottom line is that the following form does not work in NIMBLE:

 y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

It does NOT mean that it doesn't compile/run. It does run but the result is entirely wrong.

To verify this, I modified the previous code (the first post; also fixed a typo and changed some priors) and used a normal MCMC (i.e. RW sampler, not RW_PF type) for this state space model. The final results are very similar to what I expected reading Shumway & Stoffer.

Separately, I analytically derived the Kalman filter solution for this model (here I didn't include the drift term - seems to have minimal impact in this case - to make the math simpler), wrote its implementation in R and got a similar result to that of Shumway and Stoffer:

sigw: 0.05871642
cR11: 0.07400443
cR22: 0.12335148
cR12:: 0.13670587

This suggests to me that Shumway & Stoffer's estimates are correct.

One thing to note is that the normal NIMBLE MCMC is much faster (100x) than the top-down parameter estimation using Particle MCMC. Here Particle MCMC means an implementation like this:

---------------------
  N = 5000
  stateSpaceMCMCconf <- configureMCMC(stateSpaceModel, nodes = NULL)
   stateSpaceMCMCconf$addSampler(target = c('r11', 'r12', 'r22', 'tau_sigw', 'd'),
                                type = 'RW_PF_block', control = list(latents = 'x'))
  stateSpaceMCMC <- buildMCMC(stateSpaceMCMCconf)
  compiledList <- compileNimble(stateSpaceModel, stateSpaceMCMC, resetFunctions = TRUE)
  compiledList$stateSpaceMCMC$run(N)
 posteriorSamps <- as.mcmc(as.matrix(compiledList$stateSpaceMCMC$mvSamples))

-----------------------

Of course, my analytical solution with the 'optim"-based MLE is even faster than any NIMBLE solution (but I don't like the MLE approach in general ...).

The remaining question is how I can include the off-diagonal term in the R covariance matrix in the observation equation. As shown below in the code, I used on-diagonal terms only because, as mentioned, the dmnorm(mean=X[1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])  form cannot be used. Please let me know if there is a way to do this!

If this can be added to future NIMBLE development, it will be great!

Please let me know it if there is any comment or thought.

Thank you.

- Seongeun

library (nimble)
library(coda)
set.seed(1)
#
#One is globtemp, which was considered in the first chapter, and are
#the global mean land-ocean temperature index data. The second series, globtempl,
#are the surface air temperature index data using only meteorological station data.
#Conceptually, both series should be measuring the same underlying climatic signal,
#and we may consider the problem of extracting this underlying signal.

load ('globtemp.rda')
load ('globtempl.rda')

y = cbind (as.vector (globtemp), as.vector (globtempl))

stateSpaceCode <- nimbleCode({

Hi Seongeun,

Thanks a lot for posting your model and error!  I haven't yet tried the LW filter on your code, but for the second issue you posted, the following may help:

In your model code,  you define:

X [1] <- x[i]
X [2] <- x[i]

which then get used in the multivariate normal observation equation version of your model.  However, since BUGS (and thus NIMBLE's modeling language) is a declarative language, creating a single length 2 variable in your model (X) to contain all of the x[i] values from all time points will not work as expected.  That is, even though X[1] and X[2] are defined, and seemingly updated, within a for loop, their values will not necessarily be updated correctly as the MCMC algorithm runs.  To ensure that the correct values of x[i] are being passed in as the mean to the multivariate normal distribution, something like

X [i, 1] <- x[i]
X [i, 2] <- x[i]

y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

inside the for loop will work.  After this change, running your code again using NIMBLE's default MCMC gave posterior distributions for cR that seem to plausibly align with the MLE values you posted above.  Note that I used the following parameters to run the model:

USE_PRECISION = TRUE
USE_CHOL = FALSE

Let me know if you try this and it does (or doesn't!) allow you include the off-diagonal covariance term successfully in your model.  I'll also try to investigate the LW filter and see if I can figure out what's happening there.

Thanks!

Nick
